• Hoping I remembered all edge cases
• Spending 30+ minutes per review

✓ Types checking

linkedin_posts.title: My automation broke for 3 days. Here's what I learned.
linkedin_posts.body:
My automation broke for 3 days. Here's what I learned.

60 agents. All stopped. Zero errors in logs.

The silent failure that taught me the most.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝘆𝗺𝗽𝘁𝗼𝗺
Noticed on day 3: Nothing had run.
No GitHub syncs. No reports. No content.
But no errors either.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗜𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Added verbose logging.
Traced execution path.
Found it: hardcoded path to a folder I'd moved.

Scheduler tried to access: /Users/old/path
Path didn't exist.
Error was caught and... swallowed.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻𝘀

1. Never hardcode paths
Use environment variables. Use relative paths. Paths change.

2. Fail loud, not quiet
That error handler that silently catches exceptions? It's hiding disasters. Make failures visible.

3. Health checks matter
Now every agent reports "I ran" to a central log. No report = something's wrong.

4. Redundancy in monitoring
Single point of failure in monitoring = you don't know when things fail.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁
Silent failures are now impossible.
Every agent logs. Every failure alerts. Every path is dynamic.

Failures teach more than successes.

linkedin_posts.title: Your RAG system is probably broken
linkedin_posts.body:
Your RAG system is probably broken.

And you don't know it because you're not measuring the right things.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗼𝗻 𝗠𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀

• Fixed-size chunks (breaks mid-thought)
• Pure vector search (misses exact matches)
• No source attribution (can't verify)
• Giant context windows (slow, expensive)

Most RAG tutorials teach these exact patterns.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀

1. Chunking strategy
Don't split on character count. Use semantic boundaries.
Topic changes. Speaker transitions. Natural pauses.
SpaCy can detect these automatically.

2. Hybrid search
Vector search: "What's the concept?"
Keyword search: "Where's the exact term?"
Use both. My YouTubeRAG combines semantic + keyword.

3. Metadata preservation
Store source, timestamp, context with each chunk.
You'll need these for verification and navigation.

4. Test your retrieval
Before connecting to an LLM:
• Query the vector DB directly
• Check if right chunks return
• Measure precision/recall

Bad retrieval + good LLM = garbage output.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗲𝘁𝗮-𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻

RAG isn't about the model.
It's about the pipeline.

Fix chunking. Add hybrid search. Test retrieval.
Then worry about which LLM to use.

Context management is the only AI skill that matters.

Everything else is noise.

LLM performance degrades as context fills.

Every file read, every command output, every conversation turn = tokens consumed.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝘆𝗺𝗽𝘁𝗼𝗺𝘀

• Claude "forgets" earlier instructions
• Responses become confused
• Same mistakes repeated
• Quality drops noticeably

These aren't Claude problems.
They're context problems.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

1. /clear between tasks
Finished feature A? Clear. Start feature B fresh.

2. Use subagents for exploration
"Use a subagent to investigate auth."
Exploration happens in separate context.

3. Stop correction loops
Claude wrong twice? Don't keep correcting.
Clear. Write better initial prompt.

4. Keep CLAUDE.md lean
Only what Claude can't infer.
<50 lines ideal.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗲𝘁𝗮-𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻

Every AI best practice is really about context.

• Verification? Prevents context-wasting mistakes.
• Planning? Reduces wasted exploration.
• Skills? Load knowledge without bloating context.

Master context management. Everything else follows.

How I make automation survive system reboots.

The reliability layer most people forget.

Cron jobs run your automation.
System reboots.
Cron jobs need to be started again.

Except you forgot.
And your automation has been down for 3 days.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: 𝟯-𝗟𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸

Layer 1: LaunchAgent (macOS) or systemd (Linux)
• Survives reboots
• Starts automatically
• Manages process lifecycle

Layer 2: Crontab
• Precise timing (9 AM daily)
• Reliable scheduling

Layer 3: Daily Scheduler
• Orchestrates agents
• Handles dependencies
• Logs everything

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗽 (𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗢𝗦)

1. Create LaunchAgent plist file
2. Point to your scheduler script
3. Set RunAtLoad = true
4. Load with launchctl

5 minutes of setup. Infinite reliability.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁

Mac restarts → automation resumes.
No intervention needed.
No "forgot to start" moments.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗲𝘁𝗮-𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻

Automation isn't automated if it needs you to start it.

True automation = zero human intervention.

linkedin_posts.title: The best Claude Code skill is knowing when NOT to use it
linkedin_posts.body:
The best Claude Code skill is knowing when NOT to use it.

More AI isn't always better.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝗺𝗽𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

"Use AI for everything."
"Automate all the things."
"Let Claude handle it."

Sometimes this is exactly wrong.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝘁𝗼 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲

1. Simple tasks
Renaming a variable? Just do it.
Claude setup overhead > task effort.

2. Security-critical code
Auth, encryption, payments.
Human review essential. AI assistance, not replacement.

3. When you need to learn
Struggling builds understanding.
AI removes the struggle. Sometimes that's bad.

4. Creative decisions
Architecture choices. Design decisions.
Your judgment > AI suggestions.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗕𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲

Claude Code for:
• Exploration and understanding
• Repetitive tasks
• Pattern-based work
• First drafts

Human for:
• Final decisions
• Security review
• Creative direction
• Learning opportunities

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗲𝘁𝗮-𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻

AI is a tool, not a replacement.

Knowing when to use a tool is as important as knowing how.

Sometimes the right move is to close Claude and just code.

What's your human-AI balance?

#ClaudeCode #AI #Productivity #Wisdom
